title: Why Trains Refilled Water Without Stopping
topic: Why the 19th‑century American railroad company installed “water troughs” along tracks (to allow steam locomotives to refill without stopping)

lines: A fireman lowered a scoop into a trough while his train kept moving.
One long run used 1,800 to 1,900 gallons of water.
In rough weather, that climbed to 2,400 gallons.
The largest tenders held only 2,000 gallons.
Other railroad companies were slow to adopt the new device.
The locomotive passes over the trough.
The fireman lowers the scoop just before the start.
Forward motion forces water up the pipe into the tank.
Raise the scoop too late, and water soaks the tender and footplate.
You see, it's like refilling a water bottle while you're still running.
John Ramsbottom proved the method in 1860.
At 15 miles an hour, motion lifted water 7½ feet.
That height reached the top of the delivery pipe.
So trains could skip the water stop and keep their speed.
In America, big eastern railroads like New York Central and Pennsylvania used them.
The scoop sprayed water over passengers, so guards warned them to close the windows.
In America, some troughs filled with rainwater and melting snow.

claims.claim: A long run consumed 1,800 to 1,900 gallons of water, rising to 2,400 gallons in rough weather, while the largest tenders held only 2,000 gallons.
Other railroad companies were slow to adopt the water trough apparatus after the London and North-Western Railway installed it.
The fireman lowered the scoop shortly before the trough, and forward motion forced water up the scoop pipe into the tank; failing to raise it promptly soaked the tender and footplate.
John Ramsbottom demonstrated in 1860 that at 15 miles an hour the forward motion lifted water 7½ feet, reaching the top of the delivery pipe.
Water troughs let steam locomotives replenish water without stopping, and big eastern American railroads such as the New York Central and Pennsylvania used them.
Spray from the scoop could drench passengers, so guards warned passengers in the first coach to keep the windows closed.
In the United States, water troughs could be supplied by rainwater or snowmelt filling the trough during inclement weather.
